Section 1

Introduction and Scope

These notes present a compact and pedagogical review of the main physical and mathematical ingredients needed to describe absorption features produced by gas distributed along cosmological sightlines. Their central goal is to explain, carefully and step by step, how radiation emitted by a distant source propagates through an expanding universe, interacts with intervening gas, and gives rise to observable absorption signatures in the transmitted flux. Although the Ly\(\alpha\) forest provides the main physical motivation throughout these notes, the discussion is intentionally organized in a way that is also useful for related absorption processes involving metals and high-column-density (HCD) systems.

The Ly\(\alpha\) forest arises when neutral hydrogen (HI) in the diffuse intergalactic medium (IGM) imprints a dense sequence of absorption lines on the spectra of background quasars (QSOs). Because each observed wavelength can be associated with an absorption event at a different redshift along the line of sight (LoS), the forest provides a tomographic view of the high-redshift Universe. This makes it one of the most informative observables available for studying the IGM, the growth of large-scale structure (LSS), the epoch of reionization (EoR), and the connection between cosmology and baryonic physics.

At large scales, Ly\(\alpha\)-forest correlations have become a precision tool for measuring cosmological distances; at smaller scales, flux statistics such as the one-dimensional flux power spectrum \(P_{\mathrm{1D}}\) carry information about the thermal and ionization history of the IGM, the shape of the matter power spectrum, neutrino mass, warm-dark-matter scenarios, and other extensions of the standard cosmological model.

This is also why the subject is particularly timely. Modern spectroscopic surveys are now delivering quasar samples of unprecedented size and quality, and the statistical power of present and forthcoming analyses is increasingly limited not by the raw data volume itself, but by the quality of the theoretical modelling and by the control of systematic effects. In practice, one of the central challenges is no longer simply to detect the Ly\(\alpha\) signal, but to model it accurately enough that the information encoded in flux correlations and power spectra can be exploited without bias. Among the most important systematics in this context are contaminating absorption lines from metals and the impact of HCD absorbers, whose treatment is becoming essential for robust survey-grade analyses.

A useful way to think about the problem is therefore as a forward-modelling chain:

  1. Cosmology determines the underlying dark-matter distribution.

  2. The dark-matter distribution helps shape the gas distribution and its physical state.

  3. The gas properties determine the optical depth along sightlines.

  4. The optical depth determines the transmitted flux.

  5. The transmitted flux gives rise to the survey-facing summary statistics.

These notes are devoted mainly to the middle part of that chain. Our focus is on the physical and mathematical steps that connect local gas properties and atomic transition data to the observed transmitted flux, and then to the fluctuation fields and summary statistics commonly used in Ly\(\alpha\)-forest analyses.

These notes are organized so that the reader can follow the full logical chain from the basic ingredients to the quantities used in current observational cosmology. We begin by introducing the minimal cosmological background required to describe photon propagation along the line of sight in an expanding universe. This provides the geometric baseline on top of which the absorption formalism is built. We then move to the local physics of absorption, deriving how the properties of the gas and of a given transition determine the line profile, the optical depth, and the transmitted flux measured by the observer. From there, we introduce normalized flux-fluctuation fields and the summary statistics constructed from ensembles of skewers or sightlines, thereby making explicit the bridge between the underlying absorption physics and the observables targeted by modern large-scale surveys.

A second aim of these notes is to keep this formalism close to actual numerical practice. In contemporary Ly\(\alpha\)-forest work, one repeatedly needs to move from simulations or light-cone data products to synthetic skewers, optical depths, and statistical summaries that can be compared directly with observations. For that reason, the equations are presented in a form that preserves their physical meaning while also making clear how they can be organized for forward modelling and implementation. In particular, these notes are meant to accompany the development of SkewerJAX, a JAX-based pipeline for synthesizing absorption skewers from cosmological simulations and related datasets.

Finally, it is worth stating clearly that these notes are not intended as a full review of radiative transfer, nor as a complete survey of Ly\(\alpha\)-forest phenomenology. Instead, they are designed as a structured roadmap from gas and line properties to the practical calculation of the flux. The emphasis is therefore on clarity, notation, and explicit derivation.
